Text: In humans, a new strand of DNA is synthesized at {{c1::about 3000 nucleotides per minute::rate}}. DNA replication is also remarkably accurate, averaging only {{c2::one mistake per billion nucleotides incorporated::error rate}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: bacteria add about 30,000 nucleotides to a nascent DNA chain per minute, roughly ten times the human rate.

Why: speed matters, but accuracy matters even more; that fidelity is why most genes of identical twins stay identical, and the few differences trace to replication errors and other mutations.
verified_against: p240: 'In humans, the synthesis of a new strand of DNA occurs at the rate of about 3000 nucleotides per minute.' | p240: 'Indeed, the fidelity of DNA replication is amazing, with an average of only one mistake per billion nucleotides incorporated.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p240: 'In bacteria, about 30,000 nucleotides are added to a nascent DNA chain per minute.'

Text: In {{c1::1958::year}}, {{c1::Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl::two researchers}} demonstrated that the chromosome of E. coli replicates {{c2::semiconservatively::semiconservatively, conservatively, or dispersively}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: the classic density-transfer experiment: grow the cells for generations on 'heavy' medium, transfer them to 'light' medium, and follow the density of their DNA generation by generation in a CsCl equilibrium density gradient.

Why: Watson and Crick had proposed semiconservative replication from complementary base pairing just five weeks after their double-helix paper; Meselson and Stahl supplied the experimental test in E. coli.
verified_against: p240: 'In 1958, Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl demonstrated that the chromosome of Escherichia coli replicates semiconservatively.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p240: 'five weeks after the appearance of their paper on the double-helix structure of DNA, Watson and Crick published a paper describing a mechanism by which the double helix could replicate.'

Text: In {{c1::1962::year}}, {{c1::John Cairns::researcher}} demonstrated that the whole E. coli chromosome is {{c2::a single duplex::how many double helices}} of DNA.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: 'single duplex' is a claim about STRUCTURE (the chromosome is one continuous double-stranded DNA molecule), not about the mode of replication, which the density-transfer experiment had already addressed.

Why: the density-transfer result was measured on whole-chromosome DNA; knowing the chromosome is one DNA duplex lets that result be read as a statement about the DNA molecule itself, which is why the two experiments are cited together as the proof for E. coli.

Pitfall: Cairns has several separate, differently dated findings on the E. coli chromosome; keep 1962 = 'one duplex' apart from his later results on how that chromosome replicates.
verified_against: p240 (rendered page; the text layer did not locate this mark): 'Then, in 1962, John Cairns demonstrated that the E. coli chromosome was a single duplex of DNA.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p240: 'Together, the results presented by Meselson and Stahl and by Cairns showed that DNA replicates semiconservatively in E. coli.'

visual_source.note: mark not located by the text layer; sentence read verbatim on the rendered page (evidence crop work/genetics/figures/evidence/p240_mark7_cairns_1962.png, re-read by drafter-U1)

Text: Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli for many generations in medium where the heavy isotope of nitrogen, {{c1::15N}}, replaced the normal, light isotope, {{c1::14N}}. Nitrogen sits in DNA's {{c2::purine and pyrimidine bases::which part of the molecule}}, so DNA built with the heavy isotope has a {{c3::greater::greater or lesser}} {{c3::density::physical property}} than DNA built with the light one.
Back Extra:
Why: growing the cells for many generations in the heavy medium first ensures that essentially all of the starting DNA is 'heavy' before the transfer to light medium.

Mechanism: heavy isotope in every base → each DNA molecule is slightly denser → in a CsCl equilibrium density gradient, heavy and light E. coli DNA settle into two separate bands (about 1.724 versus 1.710 g/cm3).
verified_against: p240: 'Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli cells for many generations in a medium in which the heavy isotope of nitrogen, 15N, had been substituted for the normal, light isotope, 14N.' | p240: 'The purine and pyrimidine bases in DNA contain nitrogen.' | p240: 'Thus, the DNA of cells grown on medium containing 15N will have a greater density (mass per unit volume) than the DNA of cells grown on medium containing 14N.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p241: 'E. coli DNA containing 14N has a density of 1.710 g/cm3. Substituting 15N for 14N increases the density of E. coli DNA to 1.724 g/cm3.' and p241: 'cells that had been growing in medium containing 15N for several generations (and thus contained "heavy" DNA)'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: After one generation of semiconservative replication in medium containing only 14N, a parental double helix built with 15N yields two progeny double helices, {{c1::both::both or only one}} of which carry {{c1::one old 15N strand and one new 14N strand::strand composition}}. Every progeny molecule is therefore of {{c2::hybrid::heavy, hybrid, or light}} density.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: conservative replication would give NO hybrid molecules after one generation (half of the DNA still fully heavy, half fully light); dispersive replication would shift ALL of the DNA progressively lighter each generation ('half heavy' after one, 'quarter heavy' after two).

Pitfall: after only one generation, dispersive replication also predicts a single half-heavy band, so the one-generation result by itself excludes only the conservative model; the second generation (half of the DNA hybrid, half light) is what separates semiconservative from dispersive.

Ex: Meselson and Stahl's data matched the prediction: after one generation in 14N medium all of the E. coli DNA banded halfway between heavy and light, and after two generations half was hybrid and half was light.
verified_against: p241: 'One generation of semiconservative replication of a parental double helix containing 15N in medium containing only 14N would produce two progeny double helices, both of which have 15N in one strand (the "old" strand) and 14N in the other strand (the "new" strand). Such molecules would be of hybrid density.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p241: 'Conservative replication would not produce any DNA molecules with hybrid density; after one generation of conservative replication of heavy DNA in light medium, half of the DNA still would be heavy and the other half would be light. If replication were dispersive, Meselson and Stahl would have observed a shift of the DNA from heavy toward light in each generation (that is, "half heavy" or hybrid' p242: 'after one generation, "quarter heavy" after two generations, and so forth).' and p241: 'All the DNA isolated from cells after one generation of growth in medium containing 14N had a density halfway between the densities of "heavy" DNA and "light" DNA. ... After two generations of growth in medium containing 14N, half of the DNA was of hybrid density and half was light.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In {{c1::1957::year}}, {{c1::J. Herbert Taylor, Philip Woods, and Walter Hughes::three researchers}} first demonstrated the semiconservative replication of {{c2::eukaryotic::eukaryotic or prokaryotic}} chromosomes, using {{c2::root-tip cells of the broad bean, Vicia faba::organism and tissue}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the bacterial proof read out DNA DENSITY (a heavy isotope, CsCl gradient); the Vicia faba proof read out a RADIOACTIVE label: root tips grown briefly in 3H-thymidine, then followed through successive divisions by autoradiography of the chromatids.

Pitfall: the eukaryotic demonstration, in a plant, came BEFORE the E. coli density-transfer experiment; 'eukaryotic' does not mean 'later'.
verified_against: p242: 'The semiconservative replication of eukaryotic chromosomes was first demonstrated in 1957 by the results of experiments carried out by J. Herbert Taylor, Philip Woods, and Walter Hughes on root-tip cells of the broad bean, Vicia faba.' | Back Extra (unmarked, teaching only) p242: 'Taylor and colleagues labeled V. faba chromosomes by growing root tips for eight hours (less than one cell generation) in medium containing radioactive 3H-thymidine.' and 'Taylor and colleagues used a technique called autoradiography to examine the distribution of radioactivity in the chromosomes'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: {{c1::John Cairns::researcher}} established that DNA replication begins at {{c2::one unique site::one unique site or many sites}} on the circular E. coli chromosome, from which the replication of {{c2::the entire chromosome::the entire chromosome or only a segment}} is controlled.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: in the large chromosomes of eukaryotes no single site is in charge; multiple origins, sitting at specific sites, collectively control the replication of the one giant DNA molecule in each chromosome.

Pitfall: one starting site does not mean one direction of travel; replication in most prokaryotes still proceeds outward from the origin in both directions.
verified_against: p243: 'John Cairns established that DNA replication begins at a unique site on the circular E. coli chromosome. This origin of replication controls the replication of the entire chromosome.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: A {{c1::replicon::term}} is a segment of DNA whose replication is under the control of {{c2::one origin and two termini::how many origins and termini}}.
Back Extra:
Why: two termini because replication proceeds outward from the origin in opposite directions, and each traveling fork stops at a terminus.

Distinguish: an origin is a point where replication starts; a replicon is a length of DNA. Count a chromosome's origins and you have counted its replicons.
verified_against: p264: 'A segment of DNA whose replication is under the control of one origin and two termini is called a replicon.' p244: 'Each origin controls the replication of a unit of DNA called a replicon'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In prokaryotes, the entire chromosome is usually {{c1::one replicon::one or many replicons}}, whereas a eukaryotic chromosome usually contains {{c1::many replicons::one or many replicons}}.
Back Extra:
Why: a replicon is whatever one origin controls, so counting a chromosome's origins counts its replicons, and prokaryotes typically start replication from a single site.

Cue: the existence of multiple replicons in eukaryotic chromosomes was verified directly by autoradiography and electron microscopy in several different species.
verified_against: p244: 'most prokaryotic chromosomes contain a single replicon, whereas eukaryotic chromosomes usually contain many replicons.' p264: 'In prokaryotes, the entire chromosome is usually one replicon.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The single origin of replication in the E. coli chromosome, {{c1::oriC::name}}, is {{c2::245 nucleotide pairs::length}} long and contains {{c2::two::how many}} different conserved repeat sequences.
Back Extra:
Why: the two repeat classes divide the work of initiation between them: one class is where the two strands first come apart, the other is where the initiator protein docks.

Pitfall: 245 bp is the length of the whole origin, not of either repeat within it.
verified_against: p244: 'oriC is 245 nucleotide pairs long and contains two different conserved repeat sequences'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In E. coli oriC, one conserved {{c1::13-bp::length}} sequence is present as {{c1::three::how many}} {{c1::tandem::tandem or interspersed}} repeats. Because the repeats are rich in {{c2::A:T::A:T or G:C}} base pairs, they facilitate {{c3::the formation of the replication bubble::function}}.
Back Extra:
Why: A:T pairs are held together by only two hydrogen bonds versus three for G:C, so AT-rich DNA comes apart with less energy input.

Mechanism: at initiation, strand separation begins within the three tandem 13-bp repeats and spreads until the replication bubble is created.

Pitfall: the other repeat class in oriC is a protein-docking site, not the melting site.
verified_against: p244: 'One 13-bp sequence is present as three tandem repeats. These three repeats are rich in A:T base pairs, facilitating the formation of a localized region of strand separation referred to as the replication bubble.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The {{c1::replication bubble::term}} is {{c2::the localized region of strand separation}} that forms at an origin when DNA replication is initiated.
Back Extra:
Why: a localized zone of denaturation, meaning the two strands coming apart, is the essential first step in replicating every double-stranded DNA.

Mechanism: at E. coli oriC the bubble is opened by prepriming proteins binding the origin, and the initiator protein appears largely responsible for the localized strand separation.
verified_against: p244: 'facilitating the formation of a localized region of strand separation referred to as the replication bubble.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In E. coli oriC, the second conserved repeat is a {{c1::9-bp::length}} sequence repeated {{c1::four::how many}} times, {{c1::interspersed::interspersed or tandem}} with other sequences. The first step of prepriming is the binding of {{c1::four::how many}} molecules of {{c2::DnaA::protein name}} protein to the copies of the repeat, and that protein plays a key role in forming {{c3::the replication bubble::structure}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: after the first four DnaA molecules bind, more DnaA molecules bind cooperatively to form a core of 20 to 40 polypeptides with oriC DNA wound on the surface of the complex, and DnaA appears largely responsible for the localized strand separation at oriC.

Distinguish: the 9-bp repeats are where the initiator docks; the strands actually come apart within oriC's other repeat class.

Cue: 'prepriming' is everything that opens oriC before an RNA primer is laid down; DnaA protein is the product of the dnaA gene.
verified_against: p244: 'a 9-bp sequence that is repeated four times and is interspersed with other sequences. These four sequences are binding sites for a protein that plays a key role in the formation of the replication bubble.' p252: 'The first step in prepriming appears to be the binding of four molecules of the dnaA gene product—DnaA protein—to the four 9-base-pair (bp) repeats in oriC.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In prepriming at E. coli oriC, after DnaA has bound and strand separation has begun, a complex of {{c1::DnaB::protein name}} protein, the {{c2::hexameric::how many subunits}} {{c2::DNA helicase::enzyme}}, and {{c1::DnaC::protein name}} protein, present as {{c2::six::how many}} molecules, joins the initiation complex. The complex contributes to forming {{c3::two::how many}} {{c3::bidirectional::unidirectional or bidirectional}} replication forks.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: DnaA is the initiator that binds the origin first; DnaB is the helicase, and it arrives with DnaC only after strand separation has begun.

Pitfall: DnaT is also present in the prepriming complex, but its function is unknown; DNA gyrase and single-strand DNA-binding (SSB) protein are among the other proteins associated with the initiation complex.

Cue: six subunits in the helicase and six DnaC molecules, a six-and-six pairing.
verified_against: p252: 'A complex of DnaB protein (the hexameric DNA helicase) and DnaC protein (six molecules) joins the initiation complex and contributes to the formation of two bidirectional replication forks.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In {{c2::the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae::organism}}, the chromosomal DNA segments that allow a circularized DNA fragment to replicate as an independent, extrachromosomal unit are called {{c1::ARS::abbreviation}} elements, for {{c1::Autonomously Replicating Sequences::expansion}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the frequency of ARS elements in the yeast genome corresponds well with the number of origins of replication, and some have been shown experimentally to function as origins.

Pitfall: 'autonomously' describes what the circularized DNA fragment does once it carries an ARS: the fragment replicates as an extrachromosomal (outside-the-chromosome) self-replicating unit, independent of the chromosome.

Cue: an ARS element is about 50 base pairs long and carries a conserved 11-bp core sequence.
verified_against: p244: 'In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, segments of chromosomal DNA that allow a fragment of circularized DNA to replicate as an independent unit (autonomously), that is, as an extrachromosomal self-replicating unit, have been identified and characterized. These sequences are called ARS (for Autonomously Replicating Sequences) elements.'

Text: The genomes of humans and other mammals contain {{c1::about 10,000::number of origins}} origins of replication, distributed throughout the chromosomes at intervals of {{c2::30,000 to 300,000 base pairs::spacing}}.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: the number of functional replicons is not fixed: replication starts at more sites during the very rapid cell divisions of embryogenesis than in later development, and geneticists do not know what determines which origins are operational in a given cell.

Cue: Huberman and Riggs saw multiple origins directly by pulse-labeling Chinese hamster DNA with 3H-thymidine: autoradiographs showed tandem arrays of labeled segments along single DNA molecules, the sign of many origins per molecule.
verified_against: p264: 'The genomes of humans and other mammals contain about 10,000 origins of replication distributed throughout the chromosomes at 30,000- to 300,000-base-pair intervals.'

Text: The gross structure of replicating bacterial chromosomes (the E. coli chromosome, copied as a θ-shaped circle) was first determined by {{c1::John Cairns::researcher}} in {{c1::1963::year}}, using {{c2::autoradiography::technique}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: Cairns grew E. coli in medium containing 3H-thymidine so the newly made DNA carried tritium, lysed the cells gently (long DNA molecules shear easily), caught the chromosomes on membrane filters, and let the tritium's β-particles expose a photographic emulsion — the developed film traced every labeled strand.

Pitfall: the θ-shaped pictures also showed that unwinding and semiconservative copying are tightly coupled, but they could not by themselves prove how the forks move; that proof came later, from a phage λ experiment with fixed physical landmarks along the DNA.
verified_against: p246: 'The gross structure of replicating bacterial chromosomes was first determined by John Cairns in 1963 using autoradiography.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In an autoradiograph of a θ-shaped replicating E. coli chromosome, each Y-shaped structure is a {{c1::replication fork}}, and the {{c2::two::number}} Y-shaped structures move {{c2::in opposite directions::in the same direction or in opposite directions}} around the circular chromosome.
Back Extra:
Why: the θ is a circle carrying a replicated loop — the two arms of the loop are the already-copied DNA and the third arm is the stretch still waiting to be copied, so the loop grows at both of its junctions as copying proceeds.

Pitfall: the pictures only showed a shape consistent with two moving forks ('could move'); a θ shape alone cannot tell whether one fork or both are moving, so the proof came later, from phage λ.
verified_against: p246: 'Each Y-shaped structure is a replication fork, and the two replication forks could move in opposite directions sequentially around the circular chromosome (◾ Figure 10.7b). We now know this to be the case.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: An AT base pair is held together by {{c1::two::number}} hydrogen bonds, versus {{c1::three::number}} in a GC base pair, so AT-rich DNA denatures {{c1::more::more or less}} easily than GC-rich DNA, separating at a {{c1::lower::lower or higher}} pH or temperature.
Back Extra:
Why: to denature is to break the hydrogen (and hydrophobic) bonds holding the two complementary strands together so the strands come apart — a stretch with fewer hydrogen bonds per base pair lets go at a milder pH or temperature.

Ex: phage λ DNA held at pH 11.05 for 10 minutes opens only at its AT-rich stretches, forming single-stranded 'denaturation bubbles' visible by electron microscopy, while its GC-rich regions stay paired.

Pitfall: full denaturation takes about 100°C or pH 11.4; the landmark trick works precisely because a milder pH separates the AT-rich stretches first and leaves the rest of the molecule double-stranded.
verified_against: p247: 'Because AT base pairs are held together by only two hydrogen bonds, compared with three hydrogen bonds in GC base pairs, AT-rich molecules denature more easily (at lower pH or temperature) than GC-rich molecules.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In the {{c1::late 1960s::years}}, {{c1::Maria Schnös and Ross Inman::two researchers}} used the phage λ chromosome's {{c2::AT-rich clusters::sequence regions}} as physical markers in a technique called {{c3::denaturation mapping}}, showing that λ replication is initiated at a {{c4::unique::unique or random}} origin and proceeds {{c4::bidirectionally::unidirectionally or bidirectionally}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: at a mildly alkaline pH the AT-rich clusters open into single-stranded 'denaturation bubbles' visible by electron microscopy while the GC-rich DNA stays paired, so the bubbles sit at fixed, known positions along the molecule — landmarks against which the branch points of θ-shaped replicating molecules can be located.

Why: like E. coli, phage λ replicates in its circular form through θ-shaped intermediates, but its built-in landmarks let each branch point be tracked, which the earlier E. coli pictures could not do.
verified_against: p247: 'In the late 1960s, Maria Schnös and Ross Inman used these AT-rich clusters as physical markers to demonstrate, by means of a technique called denaturation mapping, that replication of the λ chromosome is initiated at a unique origin and proceeds bidirectionally.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Locating the branch points of θ-shaped replicating phage λ chromosomes relative to the fixed denaturation bubbles demonstrated that {{c1::both::one or both}} branch points are replication forks, traveling {{c1::in opposite directions::in the same direction or in opposite directions}} around the circular chromosome.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: under a one-fork (unidirectional) model one branch point would sit fixed at the origin relative to the bubbles while only the other moved; seeing both branch points shift is what rules that model out.

Why: the bubbles work as landmarks because they open only at the same fixed AT-rich spots in every molecule, so a branch point's position can be compared across many molecules caught at different stages of replication.
verified_against: p247: 'Schnös and Inman demonstrated that both branch points are replication forks that move in opposite directions around the circular chromosome.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: Phage T7, a small bacteriophage like λ, replicates its linear chromosome starting at a {{c1::unique::unique or random}} site {{c1::near one end::where along the molecule}}, so the early replicating molecule forms an “{{c2::eye::shape}}” structure.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a circular chromosome (E. coli, phage λ) replicating from one origin looks like a θ; a linear one such as T7's shows an internal bubble — the eye — instead.

Pitfall: 'near one end' is not 'at the end' — the start site sits a short way in from one end of the linear molecule, so an internal eye opens rather than a single fork starting at the tip.
verified_against: p247: 'Replication of the chromosome of phage T7, another small bacteriophage, begins at a unique site near one end to form an “eye” structure (◾ Figure 10.11a)'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The two progeny strands at a DNA replication fork are extended in the same overall direction, but because the two strands have {{c1::opposite::the same or opposite}} polarity, one is being extended overall {{c1::5′ → 3′::5′ → 3′ or 3′ → 5′}} and the other overall {{c1::3′ → 5′::5′ → 3′ or 3′ → 5′}}.
Back Extra:
Why: at the low resolution of autoradiography and electron microscopy, both nascent chains simply lengthen as the fork advances; only high-resolution pulse-labeling and density-gradient analysis reveal that one of the two strands is really assembled from short pieces, each grown in the polymerase's own direction and joined afterward.

Pitfall: 'overall direction' describes the net growth of a whole strand at the fork, not the direction in which any polymerase actually adds a nucleotide — for one of the two strands those are not the same thing.
verified_against: p250: 'Because these two strands have opposite polarity, one is being extended in an overall 5′ → 3′ direction and the other is being extended in an overall 3′ → 5′ direction.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The enzymes that catalyze DNA synthesis, the DNA polymerases, can add nucleotides only onto the {{c1::3′::3′ or 5′}} end of a DNA strand — that is, they synthesize DNA only in the {{c1::5′ → 3′::5′ → 3′ or 3′ → 5′}} direction.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: each addition forms a phosphodiester bridge between the chain's terminal 3′-OH and the 5′-phosphate of the incoming nucleotide (dTTP comes in, dTMP is added, pyrophosphate leaves), so a chain can grow only where a 3′-OH is exposed.

Pitfall: 'adds to the 3′ end' and 'synthesizes 5′ → 3′' are one statement, not two — the direction is always named by the growth of the NEW strand.
verified_against: p250: 'the enzymes that catalyze DNA synthesis (DNA polymerases) can only add nucleotides onto the 3′ end of a DNA strand—that is, they synthesize DNA only in the 5′ → 3′ direction'

Text: At a DNA replication fork, the {{c2::leading}} strand is extended {{c1::continuously::continuously or discontinuously}}, whereas the {{c2::lagging}} strand is extended {{c1::discontinuously::continuously or discontinuously}}.
Back Extra:
Cue: 'continuously' means one uninterrupted run of nucleotide additions at the strand's 3′ end; 'discontinuously' means synthesis in spurts, each spurt starting afresh, with the products joined together afterward.

Distinguish: leading-strand synthesis activity moves toward the fork, whereas lagging-strand activity moves away from it and is re-initiated on newly exposed template each time the fork opens further.
verified_against: p250: 'One, called the leading strand, is extended continuously by the sequential addition of nucleotides to its 3′ end. The other, called the lagging strand, is extended discontinuously by DNA synthesis in spurts'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In DNA replication, {{c1::Okazaki fragments}} are {{c2::the short DNA segments of the lagging strand::what, and on which strand}}.
Back Extra:
Why: the lagging strand cannot be grown in one continuous run, so each fragment is a fresh start that is later sealed to its neighbour, leaving one long, continuous chain.

Distinguish: in E. coli the fragments are 1000 to 2000 nucleotides long; in eukaryotes they are only 100 to 200 nucleotides long.
verified_against: p250: 'These small fragments of DNA have been named Okazaki fragments' / 'The lagging strand grows by the synthesis of short segments of DNA, each of which is extended by the addition of nucleotides to its 3′ end; then the many segments are joined into one long, continuous chain.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: The short DNA pieces from which the lagging strand is assembled were discovered in the {{c1::late 1960s::decade}} by {{c1::Reiji Okazaki and Tuneko Okazaki::two researchers}}, and they are named after their discoverers.
Back Extra:
Why: pulse-labeling E. coli with 3H-thymidine for only 5, 10, or 30 seconds put much of the label into small DNA fragments; a pulse-chase then moved that label into chromosome-size DNA, proving the fragments are true intermediates of replication and not a metabolic by-product.

Pitfall: the pieces are easy to miss — with longer labeling periods most of the label is recovered in large, chromosome-size molecules instead, because the pieces have already been joined.
verified_against: p250: 'named Okazaki fragments after Reiji Okazaki and Tuneko Okazaki, who discovered them in the late 1960s.'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: In DNA replication the Okazaki fragments are linked into one continuous strand by {{c1::DNA ligase::enzyme}}, which catalyzes the covalent closure of {{c2::nicks::nicks or gaps}} in DNA using energy from {{c3::NAD or ATP::two energy sources}}.
Back Extra:
Mechanism: the enzyme first forms a ligase-AMP intermediate; the AMP is transferred onto the 5′-phosphate at the nick, and the 3′-OH at the nick then attacks that phosphorus atom, forming the phosphodiester linkage between the adjacent nucleotides.

Distinguish: the E. coli DNA ligase uses NAD as its cofactor, whereas some other DNA ligases use ATP — same reaction, different energy donor.

Pitfall: DNA ligase is not only a replication enzyme — it is essential in DNA repair and recombination as well.
verified_against: p251: 'DNA ligase catalyzes the covalent closure of nicks (missing phosphodiester linkages; no missing bases) in DNA molecules by using energy from nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) or adenosine triphosphate (ATP).'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text: A {{c1::nick::nick or gap}} in a DNA molecule is {{c2::a missing phosphodiester linkage with no missing bases}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a gap is a break where one or more nucleotides are missing, not just the bond — a gap has to be filled in by a DNA polymerase before the strand can be sealed.

Why: the 'no missing bases' clause is what makes a nick sealable in a single step — there is nothing to synthesize, only one bond to re-form.
verified_against: p251: 'DNA ligase catalyzes the covalent closure of nicks (missing phosphodiester linkages; no missing bases) in DNA molecules'

visual_source.note: figure extracted from the source PDF and attached to this card (scripts/attach_figures.py --to-cards).

Text:
Every known DNA polymerase has an absolute requirement for two things in order to be active:

{{c1::a free 3′-OH on the strand being extended}}

{{c1::an appropriate DNA template strand}}
Back Extra:
Why: the enzyme's only reaction is to bridge the 3′-OH at the end of the existing chain to the 5′-phosphate of the incoming deoxyribonucleotide, and the template's base-pairing potential dictates which nucleotide that is — remove either partner and there is no reaction.

Distinguish: the primer end supplies the chemistry (a hydroxyl to bond to) and the template supplies the information (the sequence to copy) — two different jobs, both indispensable.

Pitfall: 'absolute' means no exception among all known DNA polymerases — which is the whole reason a separate priming step has to exist.

Text: Equilibrium density-gradient centrifugation is {{c1::spinning molecules until they separate by density}}.
